Guides to Historical artifacts

Books in this series are comprehensive guides to classes of historical
artifacts commonly found in excavations, archives, museums, and
private collections in North America and across the globe. Designed
for archaeologists, material culture specialists, museum professionals,
historians, decorative arts scholars, and collectors, the books explore
the interconnections between objects and social identity, and are
amply illustrated to aid in the identification and interpretation of the
technical, temporal, and diagnostic significance of objects described.
The series also serves to collate disparate and often obscure specialist
literatures and provides an arena for contributors to explore the role of
individual objects or assemblages in social action within communities.

series editors
Carolyn L. White is Assistant Professor of Historical Archaeology at the
University of Nevada, Reno. She is particularly interested in marginal
artifact types and the use of material culture to understand identity
construction.

Timothy James Scarlett is Associate Professor of Historical Archaeology
in Michigan Technological University’s Industrial Heritage and
Archaeology program. His research interests focus on material culture’s
role in the interplay of systems of cognition, belief, and economy.

introduction




For more than 30 years, the Anthropological Studies Center
(ASC) at Sonoma State University has conducted large-scale
excavations of mid-19th to early-20th-century historical archaeo-
logical sites. More than 250 archaeological collections have been
analyzed and studied from the length and breadth of Califor-
nia. The sheer volume of ceramic makers’ marks identified and
recorded has been staggering—we have identified and interpreted
marks from Germany, France, the United States, England, and
elsewhere using a wide array of references through the years.
Among these are standard resources such as Geoffrey Godden’s
Encyclopedia of British Pottery and Porcelain Marks (1991) for Brit-
ish marks; Lois Lehner’s Lehner’s Encyclopedia of U.S. Marks on
Pottery, Porcelain and Clay (1988) and William C. Gates and Dana
E. Ormerod’s The East Liverpool, Ohio, Pottery District: Identification
of Manufacturers and Marks (1982) for United States marks; and
Ralph Kovel and Terry Kovel’s Kovels’ New Dictionary of Marks:
Pottery and Porcelain, 1850–Present (1986), Mary Praetzellis, Betty
Rivers, and Jeanette K. Schulz’s Ceramic Marks from Old Sacramen-
to (1983), and Arnold A. Kowalsky and Dorothy E. Kowalsky’s
Encyclopedia of Marks on American, English, and European Earthen-
ware, Ironstone, and Stoneware: 1780–1980 (1999) for marks with
a variety of origins.
   While all of these volumes have proven useful and offer
excellent mark information, two have stood above the rest in our
work: Praetzellis et al. (1983) and Gates and Ormerod (1982).
These references provide a photograph of the mark, which has
proven to be the most effective way to identify marks, and is pre-
ferred above line drawings by the staff at ASC. This volume seeks
to offer a more comprehensive identification guide, following the
model offered by these favored guides.
     I have worked in the ASC lab for over 15 years, and this
volume is a product of those years of work. The broad geographi-
cal and temporal range of the archaeological sites studied by the
ASC enabled us to supplement, refine, and occasionally correct
these published sources on ceramic makers’ marks. It has also
permitted us to compile photographs of the marks for other
researchers. This reference manual includes a photograph of each
printed mark and line drawings of some impressed marks. The
marks studied by the ASC include well-known examples, varia-
tions of previously known marks, and formerly unidentified

                                         Each mark is clearly described using standard nomencla-
                                                   ture. A slash “/” indicates the end of a line of lettering. Symbols

                                             are in uppercase. Missing letters that cannot be extrapolated

                                     be interpolated are enclosed in brackets “[ ].” For example: (in
                                      double circle) RICHARD ALCOCK (upper arch)/ (standing
                                         Royal Coat of Arms)/ BURSLEM (lower arch)/ (in rectangle)
                                    STAFFOR[DSHIRE].
                                              Clear descriptions of the marks accompanied by photographs
                                          or line drawings will facilitate identification of marks, includ-
                                           ing fragments. The discovery of marked vessels from within
                                                 tightly dated contexts has in some cases directed research toward
                                       improving and narrowing the range of dates that a mark was
                                       used in production. The indices provided will also greatly aid the
                                               identification of marks based on the presence of a single word or
                                      group of words.

                              Marks identified
                                     The marks identified are a reflection of the contexts of the
                                            archaeological deposits in which they were recovered. During
                                           the mid to late 19th century American potters faced a domestic
                                       market that not only preferred British wares but considered them
                                            to be superior to those made in the United States. Large quanti-
                                                      ties of relatively inexpensive British wares were produced exclu-
                                                 sively for the American market, and the predominance of this
                                       market is reflected in archaeological deposits. In the late 19th
                                           century American potters began to gain recognition and more
                                        widespread regional and national distribution.
                                            Consequently, the marks identified in this volume are primar-
                                                       ily of British origin, though there are a few French and German
                                         marks. With few exceptions United States firms are excluded;
                                            these are well documented in other sources such as Lehner
                                       (1988) and Barber (1904), and Gates and Ormerod (1982)
                                       have ample photographs that cover the large pottery district of
                                             East Liverpool, Ohio. Relatively rare California marks have been
                                        reproduced here, as have several importers and retailers.
                                 A total of 343 marks can be found in this manual, of which
                                   257 have been illustrated or photographed. One hundred and
                                           twelve manufactures, importers, or retailers are represented. Of
                                                these, one hundred are British/Scottish, four are French, one is
                                    German, and seven are American (including two Californian).

How to use this Book
This book is organized alphabetically by manufacturer, and
within manufacturer by mark. Information on the manufacturer
includes manufacturer name, pottery name, pottery location,
dates of operation, previous and subsequent pottery operators,
wares produced, additional information about the firm, and ref-
erences. Mark information includes the mark description, dates
of mark use, additional comments, and references.
   For each manufacturer, individual marks are listed with an
assigned mark number. A figure number is also assigned to each
photographed or illustrated mark. Photographs and illustrations
are not necessarily to scale.
  A series of indices at the end of the book are designed to
facilitate finding specific marks or mark fragments. The first index
lists manufacturer name. The second lists town and country (or
state) of origin. The last index includes common mark elements
(seated Royal Coat of Arms, Garter, Wreath, and so on) and com-
mon words (ironstone, imperial, granite, and so on).

General comments on British Marks
Contrary to common belief, the use of the word “England” in a
mark does not necessarily mean a date after 1891, when the U.S.
McKinley Tariff Act was enacted. This act was designed to pro-
tect American manufacturers by placing high tariffs on various
imported goods and required the country of origin to be added
to imported items. More precisely, it is the absence of the word
“England” that denotes a pre-1891 date. For example, Mark 42
includes “England” in its mark even though the potter ceased op-
erating in 1876. The phrase “Made in England” was introduced
even later, in the 20th century.
   The use of the words “Trade-Mark” indicate a post-1862 date,
when the British Merchandise Marks Act was introduced, and more
likely a post-1875 date, when the act was applied to American
wares (Godden 1991:11, Kowalsky and Kowalsky 1999:577). This
act endeavored to protect British trademarks from fraud or misuse.
   “Limited,” or its abbreviation, denotes a date after 1860 and
more likely after 1880 (Godden 1991:11). Lastly, the size of the
mark has no bearing on the mark date. A mark used on a small
plate was often simply enlarged for use on a soup tureen.

the British registry diamond
Many marks include a diamond-shaped design. This “Registry
Diamond” indicates that the design or shape of the piece was
registered with the patent office in London. These registration
marks served as a form of counterfeiting protection for potters’

12  CERAMIC MAKERS’ MARKS



                                            designs/shapes. After January 1884, proof of design/form regis-
                                               tration was demonstrated by “Rd. No.” followed by a number, a
                                    numbering system that continues today. Numbers greater than
                                      351201 were registered after 1899.
                                                  Registry Diamond dates should be used cautiously. While the
                                                     initial registration of the form or pattern was good for a period
                                            of three years, the same form or pattern may have been in use
                                                   earlier or been used by another manufacturer. For example, Mark
                                        140, an October 23, 1852, Registry Diamond, was issued to Dav-
                                         enport for the “Cambridge Shape” molded pattern. This exact
                                   same pattern, now called “Scalloped Decagon,” was registered
                                     by John Wedg(e) Wood, William Davenport’s brother-in-law, on
                                       October 6, 1854.
                                          Often a pattern patent was issued to the modeler of the de-
                                                 sign, who then licensed the pattern to many potters. For instance,
                                     D. Chetwynd was the modeler of the Baltic Shape pattern pat-
                                         ented on October 25, 1855. At least two potters, George Bowers
                           & Co. (Mark 72) and Thomas Hulme (Mark 222), potted this
                                            pattern using this Registry Diamond and shape name.
                                                        Lastly, when a pottery transferred ownership, the use of the
                                               Registry Diamond may also have been transferred. Praetzellis et
                                                         al. (1980:59,78) note that Mellor, Venables & Co. (1834–1851)
                                       used an impressed mark with their name and a September 21,
                                        1850, Registry Diamond. This mark was found on four other
                                                vessels that had a printed mark from Venables & Baines (1851–
                                         1853), successors to Mellor, Venables & Co.

                                   ***

                                                          I originally envisioned this volume as a reference tool for archae-
                                                  ologists, but its audience extends far beyond. Material culture
                                                    specialists, collectors, museum professionals, students, and
                                     anyone else interested in 19th- and 20th-century ceramics is sure
                                            to find useful information here. The enterprise of archaeology
                                     mandates that this volume is not comprehensive—more marks
                                             are unearthed all the time.

about the author




erica s. Gibson spent her youth tagging along with her parents
on various archaeological sites from Nova Scotia to Alaska. She
lost her first tooth at Debert, a Paleo-Indian site, where it was
tossed in with the backfill at the end of the season. She spent
countless hours with her parents at work in the sub-basements of
the University Museum at the University of Pennsylvania and lat-
er at the Radiocarbon Laboratory of the Smithsonian Institution.
She started college with the idea of studying genetics research,
but when her entire high school chemistry class was covered in
the first three weeks of school, she hastily switched majors.

Since then, Gibson has studied the field of archaeology, spe-
cializing in the identification and analysis of 19th-century and
early 20th-century material culture. She received her MA from
the University of Pittsburgh in 1990 and moved to California in
1993. She is the Archaeological Lab Director for the Anthropo-
logical Studies Center (ASC), Sonoma State University, where she
has developed and now oversees the operation of ASC’s artifact
processing and cataloging system, SHARD (Sonoma Historic
Artifact Research Database). She also developed the “Laboratory
Methods” chapter for ASC’s “How-to Manual,” which lists the
steps to be followed in the processing of artifacts from washing
through analysis.
